title: Three upload handles verify the content hash three different ways, and hash verification is internal to the handle rather than visible to the caller
content:
`IAttachmentService` implementations each supply their own upload handle, and the handle is where transport-specific verification hides:

| Implementation | Handle behaviour |
| --- | --- |
| `SwitchboardAttachmentUpload` | streams to the switchboard's upload endpoint; hash computed **server-side inline** |
| `S3AttachmentUpload` | PUTs to a presigned S3 URL; hash verified via **`HeadObject`** after upload |
| `DirectAttachmentUpload` | streams to the local store; hash computed inline |

The design constraint this serves is stated at the top of the document: **the core interface never exposes URLs, headers, or any transport-specific detail.** The caller never sees signatures, verifiers, or presigned URLs — it calls `reserve()` and `send()` and receives a ref. That is what makes the same document model work whether Switchboard proxies bytes from a filesystem or S3 transfers them directly.

The S3 path is the one with a visible consequence, because verification requires a temporary key: the object is uploaded under `{keyPrefix}{reservationId}` (the hash is not yet known), `HeadObject` reads `x-amz-checksum-sha256` (uploads set `x-amz-checksum-algorithm: SHA256` internally so the checksum exists), and the handle then **promotes** the object — `CopyObject` to `{keyPrefix}{hash}`, `DeleteObject` the reservation key, upsert the row, delete the reservation. On dedup it skips the copy and deletes the reservation-keyed object. The payoff: every attachment ends at a deterministic hash-based key that a transport or CDN can resolve **from the hash alone, with no metadata lookup**.
